doc.title: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack") Interview, 1959-07-01
doc.interviewee: Billy McBride and Mary McBride ("Mack and Mack")

title: Mobile's brass bands: Excelsior, Eureka and Charlie Schreiner
summary: Billy recalls the Creole Excelsior band, Charlie Lipscomb and Ed Jones's Eureka band in Mobile, and how Buddy Christian and Johnny King taught them the jazz style. The Pike Theater was built for him by Charles Schreiner.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I might ask you just a minute or two, Mr. Mack, about, uh, the music in Mobile. I've heard of the old Excelsior Brass Band, and, uh, we talked to Mr. Pope, not the, I can't think of his first name. Alexander Pope was the leader of the original band. Yeah. And I talked to his son, who's still living. He's about 80 years old now.

Ha, ha, ha. But, uh, do you remember that Excelsior Band? Yeah. Yeah. I remember them for the reason that, uh, uh, in Mobile, being born, they, you know, they, they lived, uh, uh, what they called the Creoles in Mobile. They were Creoles, you know. Yeah. Yeah. And, and... Yes, he's very light. Yeah, yeah. See, and they didn't really, uh, mix too much with the rest of the colored people. And so, that's why I remember them so well. But I think this fellow, one of the musicians, who was named Willie, Pope or something like that. I don't remember very well. And we had, uh, a fellow that later became one of, that was the leader of the Eureka Band, named Charlie Lipscomb. Oh, yes. I've heard of, uh, his name. Yeah. Well, he went, uh, on my first tour out of Mobile.

I believe he's dead. Somebody told me he was, uh, Cootie Williams' teacher, I believe, too. Yeah. Did you know Cootie Williams, who played with Ellington? Sure. I know him. There's another old man whom I didn't get to meet, who still is there. I'll meet him my next trip. They called him Chicken. Some people said they could only remember his name. No. It was Chicken. Do you remember that name?
No. Well, there was a fellow called Charlie Chicken Jones, but I think he's dead.
Oh, yeah. Chicken Jones. Chicken Jones. Chicken Jones. Uh-huh.

There was, uh, some old musicians there. Uh, well, my father used to run a barbershop on Davis Avenue right down. Oh, by the way, in Mobile, there's a man, uh, I don't know, he's probably gone too. His name was Charlie Schreiner, a John Furrier-German fellow. And he built the Pike Theater for me. I just went around the country and I was having people, but they liked me so well, they wanted me to stay around, you see. And so, he said, when you come back here, I'm going to have a theater. I'm building it just because of you. And he used to loan me money too, whenever I was organizing, needed costumes and things. And I could go to Charlie Schreiner, you're in a town, a town saloon. And, uh, on account of me being always able to make enough money to pay him back, he got the idea, well, if you make money like that, I don't feel like that. Yeah. And so, all these musicians, Mobile musicians, they, they, uh, got their idea of jazz from Buddy Christian. He came over there over there. From Buddy Christian? From Buddy Christian. He'd come to Mobile and talk to the Mobile musicians how to play that style. And, of course, Johnny King, he went to New Orleans, lived a while, and he was a Mobile boy.

How did those bands compare with the New Orleans bands when you heard them later? That is, the brass band, did they swing a good deal, you know? I mean, on the street, like the funerals, you talk about coming back, you know, where they'd really swing now. Yeah, yeah. Did the Mobile bands play that same style?

They picked that up and got that out, yeah, after, like I say, the King and Christian, they kind of give them a few lessons in it, what it was all about. I was trying while talking to think of a fellow named, uh, Ed Jones, I think. He used to lead his band. He was the original, the leader of the original Eureka band, Ed Jones. In Mobile? In Mobile. And he...
Was that Eureka or Excelsior, do you remember?
No, Excelsior was this, uh... That was the Pope's band. Pope's band.
And they had a Eureka band, too. Yes. I didn't know it.
And Ed Jones used to lead the band with a baritone horn. One of them upright things, you know. Yes. And I was just over there. He did the flake jazz.

You could hear him for miles and miles. When they were coming back from the funeral. Mm-hm. And they'd step it up. About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff had a band. One time he had the Eureka band. But there always was in Mobile the same thing. Whatever happened in New Orleans, it would later get to Mobile. Like the Mardi Gras and everything.
